cards.lead: Steam trawling in the North Sea
cards.note: The Northern Mariner article dates the first North Sea steam trawl with a large winch to the Zodiac of Grimsby, built in 1881, and says steam trawlers worked from Arcachon, France, earlier, so 1881 is not the first steam trawling anywhere. The 1877 North Shields claim is not in the sources opened: the article says only that some coastal paddle tugs were fitted with trawls from 1877, with no place given.
cards.name: Steam trawling in the North Sea
cards.summary: Trawling with an engine-driven vessel from the North Sea ports of Grimsby and Hull, first applied in the Zodiac of 1881.
cards.description: The Zodiac of Grimsby, built in 1881, was the first North Sea trawler to use the marine engineering advances that made steam trawling practical. Steam trawling then spread quickly, with Grimsby having fifty steamers by 1890. Hull's first purpose-built steam trawler, the Irrawaddy, was tried from 1887.
cards.origin_note: The article reports steam trawlers at Arcachon from 1868 but does not show that the North Sea work drew on them, so the origin is not settled.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the article shows the fleet growing to nearly 1,250 British trawlers, but gives no share of people reached and says little about later fields.

events.statement: The Zodiac of Grimsby, built in 1881, was the first North Sea trawler to apply the marine engineering advances that the article links to steam trawling in the North Sea.
events.quote: Those were first applied in Zodiac of Grimsby, built in 1881.

events.label: from 1887
events.statement: Captain Dyer ran trials of the Irrawaddy, the first purpose-built steam trawler out of Hull.
events.quote: From 1887, Captain Dyer conducted trials aboard Irrawaddy, the first purpose-built steam trawler out of Hull, with her owner, George Beeching.
events.locator: Introduction to the commercial fleet, p. 335

events.label: by 1890
events.statement: Grimsby had fifty steamers by 1890 after the Zodiac's success.
events.quote: led to construction of many similar trawlers, Grimsby having fifty steamers by 1890

sources.title: The Introduction of the Otter Trawl
sources.publisher: The Northern Mariner / Le marin du nord, XVIII, No. 4

open_questions: Where the 1877 tugs fitted with trawls worked, and whether any of them were in the North Sea.
Whether the North Sea steam trawl drew on the Arcachon steam trawlers of 1868, as the article's figures suggest but do not show.
The 1881 date and Grimsby place come from the article; the Zodiac's build place is reported differently by other sources and was not checked.

cards.name: Sea-cage salmon farming on Hitra
cards.summary: Salmon reared in floating sea cages in Norway, first put into practice on a larger scale by the Grøntvedt brothers on Hitra in May 1970.
cards.description: Sivert and Ove Grøntvedt released salmon into floating cages on Hitra on 28 May 1970. Their cages were of a type built from Ingar Holberg's drawings, which he had first launched at Nordvågen in 1962. Floating cages remained the most common form of salmon farming in Norway.
cards.origin_note: The Hitra cages were built from Holberg's drawings, which is evidenced transmission of the cage design within Norway; no transmission from abroad is shown in the sources opened.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the source says cage farming is still the most common form, but gives no figures on the people it reached.

events.statement: Karsten and Olav Vik released salmon into the sea in floating boxes, a kind of precursor to cages.
events.quote: In 1959, brothers Karsten and Olav Vik from Sykkulven released salmon into the sea

events.statement: A floating net cage designed by Ingar Holberg was launched and filled with fish at Nordvågen in 1962, probably Norway's first floating cage with a net bag.
events.quote: The cage was launched, netted and filled with fish in Finnannabukta in Nordvågen in 1962 and was probably Norway’s first floating cage with a net bag as we know it today.

events.label: 28 May 1970
events.statement: Sivert and Ove Grøntvedt released salmon into floating cages on Hitra on 28 May 1970.
events.quote: Floating cages are still the most common form of operation and it was in such cages that Sivert and Ove Grøntvedt on Hitra released salmon on 28 May 1970.

open_questions: The coordinates for Hitra and Norway are approximate and were not taken from a source; they should be checked before publication.
Where the 1962 cage stood: the source gives Nordvågen but not which island or county, so the event is placed at country level.
Whether the Grøntvedt design had any link with Japanese yellowtail net cages of the 1950s, as the lead suggests; no source opened says so.

cards.lead: Mounted bison hunting on the Great Plains
cards.note: Taylor et al. (2023, Science) place horses among Indigenous peoples of the northern Rockies and central Plains by the first half of the 17th century, earlier than the lead's date, but describe them for transport, herd management and ceremony, not hunting. Hämäläinen (2003, Journal of American History) describes mounted bison chases by the Comanche after the early 1760s and a Blackfoot bison hunt around 1730, but the saved copy's lines are clipped, so no sentence could be quoted exactly. Tried: three searches, the Hämäläinen article, and a ranch site that proved unusable. A later researcher should find a complete copy of Hämäläinen and quote the 1730 and 1760s passages.

Turkey bones from central Mexico (800–100 BC) are of unclear wild or domestic status, and the El Mirador bones (cal 327 BC–AD 54) are probably imported, captive-reared birds: the authors call this indirect evidence of husbandry, not proof. The lead's claim that the turkey was the only large animal domesticated in Mesoamerica was not checked.
cards.name: Turkey husbandry in Mesoamerica
cards.summary: Turkeys in central Mexico from about 800 BC, of unclear wild or domestic status, and probably captive-reared imports at El Mirador in the Maya lowlands by the Late Preclassic.
cards.description: Mexican turkey (Meleagris gallopavo) bones from El Mirador in Guatemala, in deposits dated cal 327 BC–AD 54, show the species in the Maya lowlands about a thousand years earlier than previously recorded. The authors argue the birds were probably imported from central or northern Mexico and were kept in captivity. This is indirect evidence of turkey rearing or domestication, not proof of husbandry.
cards.origin_note: The paper says turkeys were independently domesticated in Mesoamerica and the American Southwest, but it also argues that the concept of turkey husbandry may have spread through exchange networks, so independence in the Maya case is not settled.

impact.note: Lowered from 2: the authors say turkey domestication was not widespread or common in any part of Mesoamerica until the later Classic period, and they call the El Mirador birds possibly isolated imports.

events.label: 800–100 BC
events.statement: Turkey bones at central Mexican sites date to 800–100 BC; the authors say it is unclear whether they are wild or domestic.
events.quote: In central Mexico, archaeological M. gallopavo bones have been identified at sites dating to 800–100 BC

events.label: cal 327 BC–AD 54
events.statement: Mexican turkey bones from El Mirador are dated to deposits of cal 327 BC–AD 54, the earliest turkey evidence in the Maya area.
events.quote: AMS radiocarbon ages from animal bones found in close association with the turkey remains confirm that the deposits are Preclassic (cal 327 BC–AD 54)
events.locator: Results section on the El Mirador context

events.label: cal 327 BC–AD 54
events.statement: The turkey remains show male, female and subadult birds and reduced flight anatomy, which the authors take as evidence of captive rearing.
events.quote: The presence of male, female and sub-adult turkeys, and reduced flight morphology further suggests that the El Mirador turkeys were raised in captivity.

sources.title: Earliest Mexican Turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo) in the Maya Region: Implications for Pre-Hispanic Animal Trade and the Timing of Turkey Domestication

open_questions: The El Mirador coordinates are approximate and were not taken from a source.
Whether turkeys were kept as livestock in the Maya lowlands before the Postclassic, or whether the El Mirador birds were isolated imports.
Whether the Southwest turkey domestication, which the paper says was independent, deserves its own record.

cards.note: The Nakum clay tube dates to about 100 BC–AD 250/300, but the authors say it may be a real beehive or a ceramic copy of one, and that its use is unknown. The sources support Maya keeping of stingless bees in log hives from ethnohistory, but not a documented kept-bee date earlier than this object, and whether the practice arose independently is not settled.
cards.name: Stingless beekeeping among the Maya
cards.summary: Maya keeping of stingless bees in log hives, with the earliest possible evidence a clay beehive from Nakum, Guatemala, c. 100 BC–AD 300.
cards.description: A ceramic tube from offering 9 at Nakum, Guatemala, may be a beehive or a ceramic copy of one, and the authors date it to the end of the Preclassic period. The authors say the Maya used log hives (jobon) to keep endemic stingless bees, mostly Melipona beecheii, and that beekeeping was an important Maya activity, especially in Yucatán. Whether the object was used as a hive remains unknown.
cards.origin_note: The authors do not compare Nakum with other early beekeeping or show contact with it, so independence is neither shown nor refuted.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the sources describe one contested object and a regional tradition, with no later line of work shown.

events.label: ca. 100 BC–AD 250/300
events.statement: The Nakum ceramic tube from offering 9 dates to the end of the Preclassic period, about 100 BC to AD 250 or 300 in the authors' range.
events.quote: which dates to the end of the Preclassic period (ca. 100 BC–AD 250/300)

sources.title: The Discovery of a Beehive and the Identification of Apiaries among the Ancient Maya

open_questions: The Nakum coordinates are approximate and were not taken from a source.
Whether the Nakum object was a working hive or a ceramic copy: the authors leave this open.
The Madrid Codex and the Postclassic limestone lids mentioned in popular coverage were not checked in a source with a date.

cards.lead: Systematic livestock breeding in the English Midlands
cards.note: Britannica confirms Bakewell's in-and-in breeding, culling, separation of the sexes and his work from 1760, but it does not say he was first, so the lead's first_known origin is not supported. The BAHS article on progeny testing could not be fetched, and the Darwin link and the 1790 end of the span were not checked.
cards.name: Systematic livestock breeding at Dishley Grange
cards.summary: Robert Bakewell's selective breeding of sheep and cattle at Dishley, using inbreeding and culling to fix desired traits for meat.
cards.description: From 1760, after inheriting the Dishley farm, Robert Bakewell began to innovate breeding techniques. He developed an in-and-in method of inbreeding to exaggerate desired traits, culled animals with undesirable traits, and separated male and female stock to prevent random breeding. He bred sheep and cattle for meat rather than primarily for wool or work.
cards.origin_note: Britannica describes Bakewell's methods but does not say whether earlier breeders used the same ones, so the origin is not settled.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: Britannica describes improved meat breeds and says many of his methods are still commonly practised, which supports the generativity score.

events.label: from 1760
events.statement: After inheriting the Dishley farm in 1760, Bakewell began to innovate breeding techniques.
events.quote: Upon his father’s death in 1760, he inherited the family farm and began to innovate breeding techniques.

open_questions: The Dishley Grange coordinates are approximate and were not taken from a source.
Whether progeny testing was rigorous: the BAHS article, which could not be fetched, is sceptical, and needs a copy the fetcher can reach.
Whether earlier deliberate breeding, such as Arab horse breeding or racehorse in-and-in breeding at Newmarket, would make Bakewell's method derived rather than first.
